newsitem.title: FRANCE: POLL - Highlights of French economic survey.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Highlights of French economic survey.

text.p: Following are highlights from a Reuter poll of 23 economists on the French economy (using the median forecast, mid-point of the range). Forecasts were provided between July 9 and July 16.

* GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT is seen rising 2.2 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998, just shy of this year's official forecast for 2.3 percent growth but in line with government predictions for next year.
The median 1997 forecast was unchanged from a previous April 15 survey although the 1998 forecast was up from 2.6 percent.

Economists said the more optimistic growth outlook resulted from the continued decline in the franc, which was seen having a positive impact on exports. The French currency has fallen 19 percent versus the dollar so far this year.

* PUBLIC DEFICIT seen coming in at 3.3 percent in 1997, overshooting the strict 3.0 percent Maastricht treaty criterion for joining European economic and monetary union in 1999, and only falling to 3.1 percent in 1998.

The deficit forecasts are both higher than in the last quarterly poll. Economists said this was because the new Socialist government had admitted the state of public finances was worse than previously thought and that it would not try to hit 3.0 percent in 1997 in any case.

* UNEMPLOYMENT RATE seen unchanged from the current rate of 12.5 percent in 1997 and declining to 12.3 percent in 1998. Despite government pledges to cut the jobless queues, economists expect Maastricht deficit objectives to postpone any serious attempts at job creation.
Both unemployment rate forecasts lower than previous April survey but economists said this mainly due to revisions to jobless data in June by national statistics institute INSEE.

* INTERVENTION RATE seen unchanged at 3.10 percent until second half of 1998 when interest rate rises in Germany expected to push it to 3.25 percent by the end of the fourth quarter and 3.50 percent by the middle of 1999.
Economists said European central banks likely to hold off raising interest rates until final political decisions for launch of monetary union in 1999 have been taken but then to hike key rates.
The intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, was last cut on January 30 this year.
* CONSUMER SPENDING seen climbing 1.3 percent in 1997 before picking up 2.4 percent next year. Both forecasts little changed from the previous Reuter quarterly survey.
* INFLATION seen climbing 1.3 percent this year and 1.5 percent in 1998, well within the central bank's target for inflation of two percent or less in the coming two years.
Both median inflation forecasts revised lower for the second quarterly survey in a row. Economists said this was because of a series of surprisingly weak inflation reports recently.

* FRANC/MARK exchange rate seen climbing to its central rate in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism -- 3.3539 -- in the second quarter of 1998 and staying there until the scheduled launch of a single European currency on January 1, 1999.
Economists said growing conviction single currency will be launched on time and that European central banks want conversion at central parity rates behind forecasts.
In the last quarterly survey the franc was seen at 3.3625 per mark at the beginning of 1999.

* FRANC/DOLLAR exchange rate seen stabilising in the third quarter of 1997, after sliding 19 percent so far this year to a low of 6.1720, and then climbing steadily to 5.73 by the fourth quarter of 1998.
Franc forecasts lower than in previous survey because of stronger than expected rally in the dollar against most European currencies in recent months.

* BOND YIELDS French 10-year benchmark yields seen moving from below equivalent German yields to reach parity in second quarter of 1998 and then remain at the same level until the scheduled launch of a single currency.
The yield on the 10-year French government bond, or OAT, was seen climbing steadily from the third quarter of 1997 onwards to reach 6.33 percent by the end of next year.
